## Answer

First, transposing $AC+CA=B$ shows that $C^T$ satisfies the same equation. Uniqueness therefore gives $C=C^T$. A useful representation of the unique solution is

$$C=\int_0^\infty e^{-At}Be^{-At}\,dt.$$

Indeed, differentiating the integrand and integrating from $0$ to $\infty$ gives $AC+CA=B$. For every $x\ne0$,

$$x^TCx=\int_0^\infty (e^{-At}x)^TB(e^{-At}x)\,dt>0,$$

so $C$ is positive definite. By the spectral theorem, $C=U\operatorname{diag}(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_n)U^T$ with $\mu_i>0$. Setting $\alpha_i=\sqrt{\mu_i}u_i$ gives $C=\sum_i\alpha_i\alpha_i^T$; the vectors are linearly independent because the $u_i$ form an orthonormal basis.

## Answer

Statement ① is true because $x^T(A+B)x=x^TAx+x^TBx>0$ for every nonzero $x$. Statement ② is false: two matrices that are not positive definite can have a positive-definite sum. Statement ③ is false because row full rank does not exclude a nonzero vector in $\ker A$ when $m<n$. Statement ④ is true: column full rank gives $Ax\ne0$ for $x\ne0$, hence $x^TA^TBAx=(Ax)^TB(Ax)>0$. Therefore exactly ① and ④ are correct, choice $\boxed{\text{B}}$.

## Answer

Let the three row vectors of the full-rank matrix be $r_1,r_2,r_3$. The first line is $r_3+s(r_1-r_2)$ and the second is $r_1+t(r_2-r_3)$. Taking $s=1$ and $t=-1$ gives the same point $r_1-r_2+r_3$, so the lines intersect. Their direction vectors cannot be proportional, since that would make $r_1,r_2,r_3$ linearly dependent. Hence they meet at exactly one point. The answer is $\boxed{\text{A}}$.

Therefore $\alpha_3=s\alpha_1+(1-t)\alpha_2$, so $\alpha_3$ is a linear combination of $\alpha_1,\alpha_2$. The answer is $\boxed{\text{C}}$.

Its determinant then is $-(b-1)^2$, which must vanish; hence $b=1$. Normalized eigenvectors for eigenvalues $0,1,4$ are $q_0=(-1,0,1)^T/\sqrt2$, $q_1=(1,-1,1)^T/\sqrt3$, and $q_4=(1,2,1)^T/\sqrt6$. Thus $\boxed{P=(q_0,q_1,q_4)}$ is orthogonal and $P^TAP=\operatorname{diag}(0,1,4)$.

In the alpha basis, the beta vectors form the columns of $T=\begin{pmatrix}2&0&1\\0&2&0\\2k&0&k+1\end{pmatrix}$. Since $\det T=4$, they form a basis for every $k$. If a vector has the same coordinate column $c$ in both bases, then $Tc=c$, so $(T-I)c=0$. Now $\det(T-I)=-k$, hence a nonzero solution exists exactly when $\boxed{k=0}$. Then $c=t(-1,0,1)^T$, $t\ne0$, and all required vectors are $\boxed{\xi=t(\alpha_3-\alpha_1)}$.

The symmetric matrix is $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&a&1\\a&4&a-2\\1&a-2&3\end{pmatrix}$. An ellipsoid requires $A$ to be positive definite. Sylvester's criterion gives $\Delta_1=1$, $\Delta_2=4-a^2$, and $\Delta_3=2(2-a^2)$. All are positive exactly when $a^2<2$. Hence $\boxed{-\sqrt2<a<\sqrt2}$.

At these values, $\det(\alpha_2,\alpha_3,\beta)=2\ne0$, so $\alpha_2,\alpha_3,\beta$ form a basis. Let $N=(\alpha_2,\alpha_3,\beta)$ and $S=(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3)$. The transition matrix from the former basis to the latter satisfies $S=NP$, and therefore $\boxed{P=N^{-1}S=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\-1/2&0&1\\1/2&0&0\end{pmatrix}}$.
